/publications/asymmetrical-pluralism-nor: When a speaker of Singapore English types 'Can or not?' into an AI writing assistant and receives 'Is it possible?' in return, something more than correction has occurred: a normative judgment has been rendered, algorithmically and at scale. This article examines how contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems reshape normative power in Asian Englishes through mechanisms of differential audibility. Focusing on Outer and Expanding Circle Englishes, it argues that AI operates as a normative infrastructure that mediates ideologies of correctness, fluency, and legitimacy beyond traditional institutional gatekeeping. Systematic analysis of AI outputs shows that AI privileges varieties dominant in global circulation while filtering many features of Asian Englishes into statistical marginality, routinely correcting or reframing them. This produces asymmetrical pluralism: multiple Englishes are present in AI-mediated interaction but are unevenly authorized in terms of visibility, normative weight, and legitimacy. Despite Asia's substantial use of generative AI, participation does not translate into proportional normative influence. The article concludes by calling for greater attention to audibility, norm circulation, and inequality in AI-mediated contexts.
/publications/conyo-english.pdf: This article provides a linguistic description of Conyo English, a sociolect of Philippine English marked by English–Tagalog code-switching and associated with private university-educated youth in Metro Manila. Building on Perez (1993) and Borlongan (2015), it analyzes 12.8 hours of unscripted peer-group conversation recorded by 45 undergraduates in 15 groups from four Metro Manila universities between September 2023 and January 2024. Phonologically, Conyo English shares the segmental features of Philippine English, follows Tagalog-like stress and syllable timing (with Cebuano-influenced vowels and intonation among Cebuano-background speakers), and displays a recurring intonation pattern we call the conyo contour. Lexically and grammatically, it is built on an English clause frame into which Tagalog discourse particles (na, pa, naman, diba), Tagalog verbal morphology on English stems (na-touch, mag-go), and light-verb constructions such as make + Tagalog root (make sabi) are systematically inserted. Speakers with a Cebuano background draw on Cebuano particles and syntax in parallel ways. We model variation within it as a gradient of conyoness along three dimensions, particle density, hybridization depth, and social indexical load, and argue that Conyo English is an enregistered sociolect whose emergence shows Philippine English moving from endonormative stabilization toward differentiation.
Artificial intelligence pipelines—spanning data collection, model training, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring—concentrate ethical risks that intensify with multimodal and agentic systems. Existing governance instruments, including the EU AI Act, the IEEE 7000 series, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, provide high-level guidance but often lack enforceable, end-to-end operational controls. This paper presents an ethics-by-design control architecture that embeds consequentialist, deontological, and virtue-ethical reasoning into stage-specific enforcement mechanisms across the AI lifecycle. The framework implements a triple-gate structure at each lifecycle stage: Metric gates (quantitative performance and safety thresholds), Governance gates (legal, rights, and procedural compliance), and Eco gates (carbon and water budgets and sustainability constraints). It specifies measurable trigger conditions, escalation paths, audit artefacts, and mappings to EU AI Act obligations and NIST RMF functions, enabling integration with existing MLOps and CI/CD pipelines. Illustrative examples from large language model pipelines demonstrate how gate-based controls can surface and constrain technical, social, and environmental risks prior to release and during runtime. The framework is accompanied by a preregistered evaluation protocol that defines ex ante success criteria and assessment procedures, enabling falsifiable evaluation of gate effectiveness. By translating normative commitments into enforceable and testable controls, the framework provides a practical basis for operational AI governance across organizational contexts, jurisdictions, and deployment scales.
/publications/explaining-bias-cav-nldb-2: Large language models (LLMs) often encode subtle biases that reflect historical disparities in their training data. While many studies evaluate bias solely based on model outputs, the internal mechanisms that give rise to such biases remain underexplored. In this work, the framework Bias-CAVs is proposed, an innovative framework that extends the concept activation vector methodology to probe and explain internal LLM representations for bias. This approach conducts a layer-wise analysis to quantify bias projections, revealing where bias is introduced, amplified, or mitigated within the network. In a two-stage process, activations are first extracted from key layers of diverse LLM architectures (e.g., LLaMA-3, Mistral, Phi, and Gemma) and then a linear classifier (via logistic regression) is trained on standardized activations to create Bias-CAVs that distinguish between biased and neutral representations. The findings across gender, race, profession, and political domains contribute to both the understanding of LLM internal bias propagation and the development of more explainable debiasing interventions.
/publications/how-social-media-hollowed-: The aesthetic critique of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has largely proceeded synchronically, describing what these systems produce and how they redistribute creative agency. This article argues that such accounts share a blind spot. They do not explain how audiences and creators became ready for frictionless visual perfection in the first place. Adopting a genealogical approach, it contends that the conditions for GenAI’s aesthetic ascendancy were prepared over the preceding decade of platform capitalism, which cultivated rather than merely accommodated an appetite for immediacy and legibility in visual culture. Two claims follow. First, algorithmic feedback and the quantification of approval had already converted creators’ own wanted labour into metricised, platform-facing work well before generative tools existed, so GenAI arrived as a culmination rather than a disruption, and its encroachment on creative work people wanted to do is continuous with that earlier conversion rather than a new betrayal. Second, the historically conditioned reflex equating visual sophistication with human skill persists at both individual and institutional scale after its referent has been hollowed out, and institutions now trade on that residual authority. The article introduces an ideal-conditions stipulation to separate technical and legal grievances from philosophical ones, confronts the precedent of photography directly, and argues that the emerging counter-movement toward imperfection and provenance is a coherent response to a culturally engineered condition rather than nostalgia.
/publications/instrument-object-agent-wo: This paper argues that large language models (LLMs) stand in three relations to World Englishes research: as instruments that describe, generate and annotate data; as objects whose output is a describable, standard-leaning written register; and as agents that take part in communicative ecologies and supply norms. Extending earlier work on default model behavior, it tests four models of one family against benchmarks from Peter Collins’s corpus studies of modality and the progressive. Describing Philippine, Singapore, Indian and Kenyan English, the models restated the literature’s summaries, credited claims to Collins mostly correctly but with errors that leaned toward familiar stereotypes, and often tied local grammar to low proficiency. Writing local news, they localized vocabulary but not grammar, produced no stative progressives, all but removed must from British news and omitted Philippine shall and might. Annotating modal meaning, they were highly self-consistent, with an accuracy that depended on whose definitions they were given. The paper proposes the notion of algorithmic exonormativity and closes with a reporting checklist.
